issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a rape trauma profile, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the only item that implies perpetration or morally troubling behaviour by the patient. Paired with memory items centered on terror and shame and trigger items tied to tiredness, driving with others, and sounds, this appraisal is hard to reconcile clinically with the rest of the profile and with the trauma type. The other negative appraisals reflect mistrust and loss of faith, which fit sexual assault trauma; this item instead points toward a different moral injury formulation and creates an internal mismatch within the Negative Appraisals node.

vignette: Elias had finished his final route on a Friday evening when his body first betrayed him. Eighteen hours on the wheel had left his shoulders knotted, his vision blurred, and a bone-deep weariness that felt less like fatigue and more like physical surrender. Walking from the depot to his parked sedan, he took a narrow service road behind the maintenance barn. He remembered the sudden scrape of rubber on damp asphalt, then the immediate, shocking weight of a man pressing him into the chain-link fence. Hands pinned his wrists. A voice gave sharp, demanding orders. The terror was absolute, paralyzing him in a way he had never known, and when it was over, he lay against the cold metal mesh for a long time, listening to the distant rumble of traffic, certain he would never feel safe again. The exhaustion he had felt that night quietly became a silent alarm. Whenever his body grew heavy after a long shift, his breath would catch, his neck muscles tightening as if bracing for a blow he could no longer outrun. He stopped taking service roads. He began checking his car locks three times. On his route, the sight of a passenger stepping onto the bus sent a cold wire through his chest. He told himself it was just caution, but in the quiet spaces between stops, he was certain that driving with others meant vulnerability. Certain that the space between his driver's seat and the boarding door was a boundary that could be breached without warning. When he finally allowed himself to drive his personal car again, having even a single passenger beside him made his palms sweat and his grip white-knuckle the steering wheel. At night, sleep offered no refuge. His mind would flip open like a projector, playing the service road in relentless loops. He did not just remember the event; he relived the exact terror he had felt when his body had been pinned, the same frantic pounding in his chest, the same suffocating dread. Alongside the terror came a deep, scalding shame that settled over him as the sequence replayed. He felt ashamed of his body for not fighting harder, for going limp, for being placed in that position. He had come to believe that people could not be trusted, that the world had quietly turned hostile behind his back. His faith in any higher power had evaporated alongside his sense of safety; he no longer prayed, only sat in the dark wondering why the silence had answered him with violence. Over the following months, avoidance took root. He began requesting evening routes, where the few remaining passengers were strangers he would never see again. He avoided long-haul shifts that demanded extra hours, knowing his diminishing stamina would only sharpen his fear of exhaustion. He stopped driving his personal car on crowded evenings. He withdrew from weekend dinners, from neighborhood gatherings, from the casual conversations that once filled his kitchen. His wife, Clara, noticed how he flinched when the refrigerator door shut, or how he sat rigidly still whenever a car backfired outside their window. He had not told her about the shame that clung to his skin, or how he now saw his own reflection in mirrors as something fractured. His work performance suffered not from incompetence, but from a careful, exhausting calculation of every sound on the road: the sudden hiss of a pneumatic door, the thud of a dropped bag, the specific cadence of footsteps that matched the alley that night. Now, at fifty-three, the weight of years has settled into his joints. He came to this office after Clara gently placed a referral card on the dashboard of his bus, her eyes wide with a fear that mirrored his own. He is here because the loops will not stop, because the exhaustion feels less like fatigue and more like a warning signal, and because he no longer knows how to distinguish between a present moment and a past that refuses to fade. He hopes, despite everything, that the terror might finally quiet. He fears, more than anything, that he has already ruined the safety of his own life, and that the man he was before the fence has disappeared forever.
